V8 CRANKSHAFTS / COMPARISON

Cross-Plane vs Flat-Plane V8 Crankshafts: The Complete Guide

The crankshaft changes how an eight-cylinder engine balances, alternates exhaust pulses between banks, and responds as engine speed rises.

01Cross-plane90° crank-pin spacing
VS
02Flat-plane180° crank-pin spacing

INTRODUCTION

The crankshaft in 60 seconds

A four-stroke V8 completes one full 720° combustion cycle across its eight cylinders. That means eight firing events, spaced at 90° of crank rotation in both cross-plane and flat-plane layouts.

The crankshaft geometry does not change that global 90° interval. It changes which cylinder bank produces each event and how the crank's rotating and reciprocating masses are arranged.

Key correction: do not describe cross-plane V8s as globally “uneven firing.” The firing interval is even. The unevenness discussed here is the alternation between banks.

01 / CROSS-PLANE

Cross-plane

Cross-plane crankshafts place crank pins at 90° intervals, creating two perpendicular crank-pin planes. A common Chevrolet small-block example uses firing order 1-8-4-3-6-5-7-2.

Cylinder numbering convention: Chevrolet small-block — left bank 1-3-5-7; right bank 2-4-6-8.

Mapping that firing order to those banks gives L-R-R-L-R-L-L-R. Some consecutive events therefore arrive from the same bank.

90° pins
1–8–4–3–6–5–7–2Chevrolet SBC firing order

02 / FLAT-PLANE

Flat-plane

A flat-plane crankshaft places its crank pins 180° apart in a single plane. With an appropriate V8 firing sequence, the exhaust events alternate banks, producing evenly spaced pulses in each bank's exhaust stream.

SOUND

Why the sound differs

The crank layout is a major factor because it changes the sequence in which each bank's exhaust pulses arrive. A flat-plane V8 can present evenly spaced pulses to each bank, while a cross-plane arrangement can group pulses on a bank before a longer gap.

That is only part of the sound. Exhaust design also matters: manifold length and geometry, collector arrangement, and systems such as 4-1 or 4-2-1 layouts reshape the pressure waves before they reach the tailpipe.

APPLICATION

Real-world use

Cross-plane crankshafts are common where smooth primary balance, broad road use and manageable NVH are important. The additional crank mass and exhaust-pulse grouping are accepted as part of the architecture.

Flat-plane crankshafts are associated with high-performance V8 applications where lower rotating inertia and evenly alternating bank pulses can support the desired engine response and exhaust behavior. Second-order vibration is a design consideration handled through the engine structure and mounts.

MYTHS

Common myths

Myth: “Cross-plane V8s fire unevenly.”
All eight events still occur every 90°; bank alternation is what becomes irregular.
Myth: “The crankshaft alone creates the sound.”
Crank layout matters, but exhaust manifold geometry and pulse routing also shape the final sound.
Open marker: [VERIFY] Any model-specific claim should be checked against an engine-specific technical source.

Head-to-head table

INTERPRETATION

Verdict

Neither crank layout is universally superior. The geometry changes counterweight needs, vibration characteristics, exhaust-pulse sequencing and packaging choices; the complete engine determines the resulting behavior.

For this guide, the useful distinction is not “uneven versus even firing.” Both V8 layouts have one firing event every 90° of crank rotation. The key difference is how those events alternate between the two banks.
